utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The Chamber has advanced the start of trial for today by half an hour to 8.30 in order to have more time for Defence case, if any; but however, first of all I'd like to hear from the Defence adds to their position in relation to their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Very briefly and quickly I shall present the position of the Defence. The joint position at that, so I'm speaking on behalf of Mr. Ivanovic and in my own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continuing in the spirit in which we started this hearing and after consultations with our clients and after having heard the evidence called by the Prosecution, the Defence came to the conclusion that there is no need to call any further witnesses because, in relation to the witness, Mr. Tomljanovich, we actually have nothing to elaborate on. We consider it superfluous, this particular evidence, unnecessary; and, in fact, we have nothing to oppose. As for the evidence given by Mr. Cameron, we consider it to be useful and we think that this Prosecution witness actually confirmed, in part of his testimony he even clarified, what the Defence possibly wanted to prove through its own witnesses. So basically these are the main reasons why we consider it unnecessary to call further evidence in the spirit of flexibility, in terms of calling new witnesses on our side, that is. On the other hand, in line with your decisions on admitting evidence without witnesses - I'm talking about documents now - I would kindly ask you to admit these documents because they are actually court documents. In actual fact, these are two decisions of the Blaskic Trial Chamber, the President of that Chamber was His Honour Judge Claude Jorda. These are two orders on protective measures, and through them we wish to show clearly what the Trial Chamber was guided by, very clearly, and they set the rules. This has to do with the evidence of General Morillon, the former UNPROFOR commander; and Messr Jean Pierre Thebault, the high representative of the United Nations; they both testified in the Blaskic case. The Court clearly reached its decision to have a closed session, but the Court also set the clear-cut rules in terms of protecting the content and that neither the Prosecution nor Defence -- nor the Defence can ever disclose any of this evidence, but there's no need for me to go on about this at length. In contrast, their names were not protected, that is to say it is a matter of public knowledge that they testify, but the content of their testimony is protected. We are showing this because the testimony of Mr. Van Kuijk never had this kind of supporting decision on protective measures. Had this been necessary, the Chamber certainly would have issued this kind of separate order. Therefore, we assert, we assert - and that is clearly based on these documents which I kindly ask you to admit - that protective measures in the case of Witness van Kuijk actually never existed. I have copies for all the parties involved and for yourselves, Your Honours, so please kindly have a look at this and could you please have this admitted into evidence. This is all I had to say and I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could those two documents be handed over to the Bench, and in the meanwhile we would like to hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No objection to the admission of these documents whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit them. Those will be given numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The first decision dated 12th of May, 1999, will be allocated the reference number D1. The second decision dated 30th of May, 1990, will be given the reference D2. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we go into closing arguments, starting from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry. I can't see the transcript on this screen, so if the gentleman could assist me. I have no transcript, so perhaps it's a technical error. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Akerson, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: May it please the Court. On November 18th, 2004, Hrvatski List published two articles which sensationally and dramatically exposed the identity of an ICTY witness as well as the content of his closed-session testimony. The articles brazenly challenged the authority of this Tribunal and its ability to protect the confidentiality of its witnesses, and in so doing it interfered with its administration of justice and its contempt of Court. I just want to remind Your Honours that we are going to be showing slides, so if you could have your monitors turned on to computer evidence. The facts of this case are largely undisputed or I should say are undisputed. In December of 1997, Johannes van Kuijk, a Dutch peacekeeper, testified in the Blaskic case in closed session and his identity was never publicly revealed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say the facts are not in dispute, I have to make reference to a point which seems fundamental and you could perhaps at an early stage clarify it for me. You produced a document yesterday which is samples of common evidence between the closed-session testimony and the ICTY witness statement. How much of this material is actually in the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The article publishes most of the witness statement and -- I think I discussed this in the closing argument and I will address this issue, but the witness statement merely in its entirety is published in the Hrvatski list article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Marijacic was the editor-in-chief of Hrvatski List, and he was the author of the articles in question. In the main article he published the identity of van Kuijk by name. He published his statement which is flagrantly touted on the cover of the issue as a secret document in bold, large, and red font. He referred to the fact that the witness had testified secretly, and the words "secret document" are peppered throughout this issue. In the accompanying document Markac identifies Markica Rebic, and Rebic states that he provided Hrvatski List with both the transcript and statement of van Kuijk. He states that he knew the documents were protected. If you look on your screen you can see that clause. "Are these protected documents and what do they represent?" "They are protected documents and I am aware of the possible consequences of them being revealed to the public. Such documents have occasionally appeared previously, but their publication might be regarded as obstructing the work of the Office of the Prosecutor or the Court," which is almost exactly tracking the language of interfering with the administration of justice, obstructing the work of the Office of the Prosecutor or the Court. In April, Marijacic and Rebic are indicted and a short time after that they both defiantly repeat their admissions. On March 7th, Marijacic gives an interview to the Croatian press agency HINA and in this article he reaffirms that he knew he was disclosing a protected ICTY witness statement and a witness. And if you can see the slide. A short time later on May 5, 2005, Marijacic dedicates an entire issue of Hrvatski List to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've lost your timing there. You say in April they were indicted and then in March Marijacic gave the interview to HINA. Are these dates accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The indictment is issued in April. Shortly thereafter Mr. Rebic gives an interview to the HINA news agency. In May about a week after that, an issue of Hrvatski List is dedicated to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Right, the transcript says "March 7," it should say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It also says "Marijacic," and it was Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It's -- Rebic on April 27th gave an interview to HINA. In the May 5th issue of Hrvatski List Marijacic states that -- when handing us the document to read at Hrvatski List in November last year, Mr. Rebic said that he knew it concerned a protected witness and testimony "Having pondered at length the pros cons of publishing it, we opted for the latter, publishing the document at this time," and then it goes on. The next quote Marijacic adds: "In addition, in Croatia -- in addition, in Croatia, we have earlier been getting away with revealing protected witnesses. For example, immediately after," and then they, Marijacic lists another protected witness in the Blaskic trial. "Immediately after that protected witness had testified in secret in The Hague against Croatia and General Blaskic, many in the Croatian media had published his identity and also the content of his testimony." These basic facts form the crux of its case. Now, in order to enter a conviction against Marijacic and Rebic, this Chamber must find that the Prosecution has proved under Rule 77(A)(ii) three things: One, that Rebic and Marijacic knowingly and willfully interfered with the administration of justice by disclosing information relating to those proceedings, in knowing violation of a court order. And I'll take each of these three elements in turn. First, the Prosecution must establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Rebic and Marijacic knowingly and willfully interfered with the administration of justice. Now, by intentionally violating a court order, which they admit they do, Rebic and Marijacic interfered with the administration of justice. The Prosecution would submit it's a per se interference with the administration of justice when they intentionally interfere or intentionally violate a court order. Now, the public and defiant nature of their challenge to try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you -- sorry, Mr. Akerson. You say that that applies even though the order is serving no useful purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I don't believe the order is serving no useful purpose. I would contest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you unable to say what that purpose was?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I will get to that in my closing -- I mean, I can address it right now. The purpose is that we have a trial dealing with Croatian witnesses and a newspaper that brazenly and defiantly challenges our witness protections. In this case, the most serious protection we can afford a witness undermines our ability and your ability for us to bring in witnesses and ensure them that their confidentiality will be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different matter. That argument I understand. My question to you is: What useful purpose was this order actually serving at the time the publication took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Are you referring to the oral order to move into closed session testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That order was decided by the court based on the arguments of the parties. I think at this point you can't second-guess that order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The publication is seven years later. I want to know what useful purpose at the time of publication that order was actually playing or had it just been left there and everyone had forgotten about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: But the issue at stake is are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not seven, four years later. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Clearly the content of his testimony was protected and they published the content of his testimony; that's undisputable. Now, the question is, was his identity protected? And I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. That's not the -- the question is -- it goes further than that. The identity issue's a separate one. What purpose was being served at that stage by protecting the content of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, in 2004 when the alleged breach takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution would submit that it doesn't matter -- even if it did matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate argument. Tell me what useful purpose the order was actually fulfilling as at the date on which the publication took place. Why was it still in force? Or indeed was it still in force?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It has to be enforced until the -- nobody can lift -- it would be our submission that no one except for a Trial Court can modify that Trial Court's order. I mean, what -- I think the argument that you're raising, Your Honour, is that Trial Chamber orders can be second-guessed by anyone if they can look at a transcript and determine for themselves that they think the order was wrong. Let's presume the order was entirely wrong from the beginning in this particular case, does that mean that newspapers can look at it and say: That order of the Trial Chamber was wrong, therefore we don't have to obey it. I mean, I think that's the principle at stake that you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate matter. What I would like -- still would like an answer to is the question: What useful purpose that order actually was serving as at November 2004? Or would -- if the Prosecution had seriously reviewed the position, would they have had it revoked by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: But it -- from our perspective, Your Honour, it doesn't matter because what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can't answer the question. That's fine. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The public and defiant nature of the challenge to the Tribunal's ability to ensure witness confidentiality is a serious interference with the administration of justice. Witnesses face deadly risks by coming in to give testimony at this Tribunal and often they can only testify confidentially. Meaningful and enforced confidentiality measures are critical. Hrvatski List publicly challenged these protections, serving to undermine, one, the Croatian public's confidence, and thus seriously interfered with the administration of justice and seriously interfered with our ability -- in the period of time before a large Croatian case is going to be tried at this Tribunal, our ability to bring in witnesses and assure them that their confidentiality measures will be protected and enforced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we simply have to take your word for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: On what -- on what issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About the actual interference, you say this, or the breach caused with the administration of justice? You're saying it actually interfered with the conduct of a later case that was about to start at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis -- where's the evidence for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The evidence is the issue of the newspaper itself which openly and brazenly challenges the authority of the witness protection scheme and puts it into the marketplace of Croatia, in newsstands all over Croatia. I think that is res ipso loquitur, it speaks for itself. The next element that the Prosecution has to prove is that Rebic and Marijacic disclosed information relating to the proceedings. The proceedings in this case are the Blaskic proceedings, and I think that's indisputable. Van Kuijk is a witness in the Blaskic case, the orders that apply in this hearing are from the Blaskic case. Everything pertains to the Blaskic case. The last element is that the Prosecution must establish that Rebic and Marijacic disclosed information knowingly violating a court order, and I think that's where this case turns. There are two court orders: One is the oral order to proceed under closed-session protections on December 16th, 1997; and a second written order on December 1st 2000. I'll take those in turn. You have in front of you on the screen the oral orders, and you can see that it's repeated frequently and in fact on every page of the transcript where it is in closed session. It repeats "this is closed session testimony, closed session testimony." Now, Rebic and Marijacic clearly knew about the oral order to proceed in closed session. Rebic admits delivering the physical transcript to Mr. Marijacic. Marijacic admits to receiving the transcript. The transcript contains repeated references to the fact the testimony was closed. Now, Rebic and Marijacic violated this order very clearly by publishing van Kuijk's statement. As I've submitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, for the sake of the Bench, if you could wrap up your evidence for the fact that Mr. Rebic disclosed this transcript to Mr. Marijacic. What evidence do you have? What evidence has been tendered to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That Mr. Rebic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Disclosed the transcript to Mr. Marijacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We have there, one, the article on November 18th, 2004, in which it's published and they admit that in an interview. If you put that up on the screen. Interview of Mr. Rebic, he says: "What are these two documents?" There is a witness statement of van Kuijk and his testimony and I'm handing them to Hrvatski List. And then he goes on to say -- or the interview goes on to say: "Are they protected?" And he says, "Yes, they are protected. I know they're protected." And you've seen the quote before where she says "is obstructing." And he says, "Yes, it could be seen as obstructing the work of the Tribunal." So you had that admission, first. Now, if you want corroboration, they've actually published the witness statement. So that corroborates his own admission, "I've turned over these two documents and we've decided to publish the statement." So it's corroborated by the fact they did publish his statement. Then on April 27th, Mr. Marijacic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Rebic gives an interview to HINA where he confirms: "Yes, I turned it over and I knew what I was doing and I knew it was protected." What's important to note is that Mr. Rebic at that point has gone from just being somebody who turns over a transcript and a witness statement to somebody who is now employed by Hrvatski List. So if it's the suggestion of this Chamber that it's not reliable that this publication had printed their own admission that it was turned over and they were in possession of it, you would think that Mr. Rebic would not want to be associated with the publication that had defamed him and made up false accusations about whether he turned these over. Mr. Marijacic also confirms, "Yes," this is on May 5th in a second Hrvatski List, Mr. Marijacic confirms it and says: "Yes, it was turned over to us by Mr. Rebic." There were no retractions issued by Hrvatski List, no subsequent publications. So it's very clear on the face that it was an honest and accurate statement, and I think that's the only logical inference that can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in sum, you are asking the Chamber to rely on those newspaper articles to convict the accused, which the accused themselves do not admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I don't think there is any real challenge to the authenticity of these articles, but, yes, the crux of this case is formed on November 18th, the edition of Hrvatski List, then the HINA Article that's on April 27th, the May 5th article, and the fact that there is no retraction issued in each the subsequent editions of these articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson, please go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the connection between Mr. Rebic and the management of Hrvatski List?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In the May 5th edition of Hrvatski List in the header it now lists Mr. Rebic as, I think, editor-at-large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just one other matter. Is there a principle in a case involving two accused that a statement by one of them without the presence of the other is not evidence against that other? In other words, where you accuse Mr. Marijacic and the person he interviews and you base that accusation on what Mr. Marijacic writes, can you actually use that as evidence against Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would submit that you can when it's adopted by both parties in subsequent publications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We were talking about the oral order and the fact that Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic knew that the oral order existed. It protected the content of van Kuijk's testimony. They published his witness statement, and so the issue for this Court is: Does publishing the witness statement actually amount to publishing the content of the testimony. And you've argument about this earlier in this trial, and the question is: Does -- when you move into closed as a Chamber, are you protecting just the literal transcript or are you protecting the content of what that witness testifies to? And it would be the Prosecution's submission that the only logical inference can be that the content of what he's testifying to is protected. And I would say that if I was interested as a newspaper in publishing protected witness information that he testified to, a witness's testimony that was in closed session, it's a much more effective vehicle to publish his statement when it mirrors his testimony than the actual transcript. The transcript is long, it's filled with objections, there's lots of side-bars, it doesn't follow in a logical sequence. The witness statement, on the other hand, is short, it's dense, and it contains all of the key areas that the witness is going to testify to or what is relevant about that witness. And Your Honours are well aware that many examinations, direct examinations, the witness statement is actually used as the template for examining the witness, so they often mirror each other. And certainly you have evidence in front of you in this case that are largely similar and you have evidence in front of you that the intent, that the intent of Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic was to publish his protected testimony because they say that. And they did it by publishing his witness statement which is a much more effective vehicle than publishing his transcript in this case. But the bottom-line principle is that: When you move into closed session with a witness, what he testifies to is protected, no matter what form it occurs in, whether it is a summary or a statement which they know to contain the same information. So by publishing his witness statement in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say it's a more effective vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say publishing the witness statement is a more effective vehicle than publishing the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In a statement, a witness may say: I saw a particular event. When he testifies, he might get asked a question, there may be an objection, and so the transcript will then have two pages of argument about the objection. The witness then, when he's refreshed about the question, may say: I don't remember the question, can you rephrase? The transcript may go on for pages before the witness answers. So what you have oftentimes, and I would say most often, is many more pages of a transcript to cover the same information, whereas the witness statement, it's down to one paragraph usually, or a very short, concise detail of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I was misled by the epithet "effective." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Well, based on what I just said, I think it's very clear when they published his statement they violated the oral order of -- oral order on Mr. Van Kuijk that he proceed in closed session. The last issue about the oral order is whether or not they violated the oral order by disclosing his identity, and that's an issue that Defence counsel has just raised. The question is: Do -- when there's an oral or a written order to proceed in closed session, does that automatically guarantee the witness's -- or does that automatically protect the witness's identity? And I think the case cited by Defence counsel supports our proposition. It automatically supports the content of his testimony. It usually protects his identity, but not always. In the case of General Morillon, the Trial Chamber listed him as a witness. First they listed a number of witnesses, including General Morillon, by name and said: "If you would like protective measures, please apply to the Court." So his identity was revealed first and the request of the witnesses to seek protection measures was later. So in that particular case, it's very, very clear that the only thing that was protected was the content of General Morillon's testimony, not his identity. Very different from the factual situation you have. In this case, Mr. Van Kuijk's identity is never revealed in open session, not on one occasion his identity revealed in open session. The attorney and Judges do not use his name and they're very careful to refer to him as "witness" when arguing whether or not he should testify in closed session. Then when they proceed to and they are in closed session, they then use his name. So it's very clear they are intending to protect his identity. So on these facts with this transcript that was in the possession of Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic, it was very clear that the identity of Mr. Van Kuijk was protected and it was protected for the seven years after that until Hrvatski List published it. They knew it, they state it, admit -- they admit it in their publications, the first and second publications. You also have evidence introduced by Mr. Tomljanovich that back as far as 1997, 1998, Mr. Rebic was advising others that with these closed-session witnesses the identities are protected as a general rule. I'm just saying this: Your Honours are far more familiar with closed-session procedures than I am, but closed session is the most extreme form of protection that a witness can get. The screen is pulled down, the public is precluded from seeing anything about a witness. So the general rule has to be that closed session -- the intent of closed session is to protect the witness's identity, unless it is clear that the contrary is intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One -- there is one peculiarity, though, that perhaps you can deal with. How was the witness listed? How was he identified in any list of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The witness was not listed in the original witness list; he was brought up as an addition to the witness list in open court on the record. And he was always referred to in that context as "this sensitive witness."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you know that that in itself may be an exceptional circumstance, that witnesses who are protected -- whose identities are protected are usually given pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think in this case he was later given a pseudonym, but at this time he did not have a pseudonym and the record doesn't have any record of a pseudonym. He was always referred to as a "sensitive witness" or a witness, until they moved into closed session and then he was referred to by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that you think that later in the case he was given -- he might have been given a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be very helpful to me if that were so.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Later on he was assigned a pseudonym, yeah, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, but I would have no problem with that -- it's a court record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but then you must show us.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I only saw it yesterday when the Court had asked whether there were additional protective measures. I -- what I -- yesterday I had spoken to the senior trial attorney that had been involved in that case, and this was a very brief conversation that took place on a break, but it seemed that the pseudonyms in the Blaskic case were for the purpose of the submissions at the end of the case so that you could refer to the testimony because there wasn't the pseudonym structure in place during the time of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I -- speaking for myself, I would like to have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I will be happy to provide that to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would be very interested in seeing that, because it would help me to decide whether the -- there was an intention to protect the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll be happy to provide that, but -- we would submit that the record, the oral order in the transcript is very clear that the intent of the parties was to protect his identity, and that's what was in the possession of Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic. That's what they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the moment, I have to say it's not as clear to me as it obviously is to you. This seems to me to be a rush job that was done without much thought at the time, unlike the way in which the orders in relation to Morillon and Thebault were handled. And then I wonder if you are going to suggest that there are other examples of witnesses who are public officials out with -- residing only out with the former Yugoslavia through which this sort of order would normally be regarded as covering identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say, "this seems to be a rush job," are you referring to the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: -- to award Mr. Van Kuijk protection measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He seemed to arrive without warning. Is that wrong? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: He was discovered by the Prosecution in 1997 at a late stage and was added -- the argument that takes place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How was he added -- if he didn't have an identity, how was he added?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: What happened is that the Prosecution said: We have a sensitive matter we would like to discuss in closed session. There was argument that was conducted in closed session. His name at that time -- this was before the date that Mr. Van Kuijk testified. His name was never revealed in that discussion, and in fact the argument centred on providing the Defence with a redacted witness statement of the sensitive material in that particular case. But he was added on the fly as a newly discovered witness. Within a few days he was testifying. All the argument that took place referred to him as: "Witness protecting his identity." And the only time his identity was ever revealed was when they went into open session when he actually testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, you are fairly well-resourced. I would suggest that you have one of your assistants investigate the matter as to whether they -- the witness was later given a pseudonym so that you can bring that so our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can do that at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Shall I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: So I just discussed the evidence regarding the oral order, so I'm now going to move to the written order of December 1st, 2000. Now, if you can place the order of December 1, 2000, on the screen, please. The operative order in this case was issued against two newspapers where -- one of which is where Marijacic worked at the time. And the order, the operative order, states that "the publication of statements or testimonies of the witness concerned and of any protected witness shall cease immediately and states that any publication of these statements or testimonies shall expose its authors and those responsible to be found in contempt of the Tribunal." So under Rule 77(A)(ii), the Prosecution has to prove knowing violation of this order. So the first question is: Does this apply to Mr. Van Kuijk because it applies to protected witnesses. Now, the Appeals Chamber has recently ruled that he was a protected witness; so that's not an issue. And we know that Mr. Marijacic published Mr. Van Kuijk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Appeals Chamber say so? There were protective measures, but I don't think it said Mr. Van Kuijk was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll have to review the exact wording of that. It would be our submission anyways when they say "a protected witness," they -- it's inclusive anyways, and the clear intent was a broad expression to try and stop the leak of information that was occurring at the time with the two newspapers. Mr. Marijacic published the statement, so that's clear. Mr. Rebic admits delivering the material to a newspaper. Clearly we knows that -- and they state that they deliberate about publishing the material. So he is collaborating in the process of the publication. So he would fit into the last phrase "those responsible for publication." So the only legitimate issue the Prosecution would argue that could be raised by Rebic and Marijacic is whether they had knowledge of this order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Akerson, Mr. Rebic was not indicted for having collaborated in publication of these statements. He was indicted for disclosing these materials. So how then you can say that Mr. Rebic has violated the third order of 1st of December, 2000, in terms of -- consider -- given the context of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. In the indictment he's charged with disclosing information, which violates this order. Now, this order says: "Those responsible for the publication of statements or testimony," so you have the publisher plus those responsible. By him disclosing to a newspaper and the clear evidence that you have from their own statements in the newspaper is that the intent of him providing this to a newspaper is that it's going to be published. So he is, in effect, he is publishing by disclosing. So he disclosed the information to a publisher which invokes this order. That's the submission of the Prosecution on that point. So the question becomes: Did Mr. Marijacic and Mr. Rebic have knowledge of this order? Now, we know that Mr. Marijacic worked Slobodna Dalmacija in December 2000 as an editor. You've heard evidence of Terry Cameron and you've seen issues that are in front of you, the issues of Slobodna Dalmacija, that the cease and desist order, this very order, this one of December 2000 was directed on and served on Slobodna Dalmacija after they had published over four days the witness statement of a protected witness, a different protected witness. Now, Slobodna Dalmacija then published the order in its entirety in an issue and then dramatically pronounced that they were defying that order and ran a series of articles until the end of December. So this starts on November 26th and goes until the end of December. In addition to publishing the order in its entirety, they repeatedly refer on the cover of Slobodna Dalmacija to the existence of the order that's been served on them. Articles inside the editions, 22 editions in all, reference the order and the protection and the issue of the Tribunal issuing a cease and desist order against this paper. So the only reasonable inference the Prosecution would submit that can be drawn is that Mr. Marijacic read the paper he worked for and he was aware of the prominent story which centred on a cease and desist order served on that paper. And moreover, Mr. Marijacic contributes, as you have a table in front of you, many articles that are related and oftentimes are in juxtaposition to the published, protected transcript. So he's participating in this series of articles. So Mr. Marijacic's knowledge of this December 1 order, the Prosecution would submit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it is civil to interrupt a closing argument, but I do have to, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Only if you think the evidence is being misstated, otherwise I would suggest you wait for your closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will wait then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that a conclusion was wrongly drawn that Mr. Marijacic wrote anything about that testimony. You have all the material in front of you and you can see that not a single text written by Mr. Marijacic refers to the testimony of that other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Defence will have time to rebut that allegation. So Mr. Akerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: So the inference, the only logical inference, the Prosecution would submit, that this huge story that runs over six weeks in this newspaper centred around the disclosure of protected witness and his -- and the publication of his protected testimony. And Mr. Marijacic worked for that newspaper; he would have clearly known of this order. And I would just also point the Court towards the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Aleksovski contempt case, that even if this Court -- if you want to draw the inference that he was working for a paper and he was writing articles that -- they weren't directly commenting on the testimony, but they were related to the protected witness and they were clearly in a position that showed that he was participating in the series of articles. But if you only want to infer that he was aware generally of this order - and it's hard to make any other inference but that because this story runs for six weeks, this is a huge paper -- this is a huge story and a huge paper - the willful blindness issue in the Aleksovski case says: If a person chooses to blind himself of an order, he cannot escape its provisions. So either -- I mean, the Prosecution would submit it's clear that the logical inference is that he's got actual knowledge of this order but, in addition to that, even if he has only a general knowledge or a general memory of this order, he can't blind himself to that fact in 2004 when they're considering whether to publish the protected witness testimony. And he knows generally of this order. He's charged with having actual knowledge of it under the willful blindness doctrine if he chooses just not to refresh his memory. And it's easy for him to refresh his memory because he worked for the paper. He knows how to get a copy of the edition that has the order printed in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say was his precise work for the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: He was an author. He was writing articles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was a contributor?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: He was contributing articles. He contributed 11 articles during that series. And as I said, the articles were articles about the witness who is a protected witness, and they are oftentimes right next to -- you can look at the editions and see because the position of these articles is, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was he a part of the management of the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We don't have any evidence that the banner of the newspaper does not indicate that he was part of management. All we know is that he was authoring articles, and in fact he stipulated that he was employed by Slobodna Dalmacija at the time. What his official title was, I don't know. I do know -- I don't think it's really relevant because he was writing articles. He is a journalist. He was writing articles at the time. In a series of articles about an order -- and what's important is: Did he have knowledge of the order? And no matter what capacity he's working in -- if he's a journalist and his paper is focussed on this court order, I think the logical inference is that he's reading his own paper, especially with a huge story like this, a dramatic story where the paper is challenging the Tribunal's very authority publicly. Here's the order they served on us. We're not respecting it. We don't think they have the authority to -- to tell us to stop publishing protected witness information. I mean, it is a big story for them. I think the only reasonable inference can be that he was reading -- he was reading and following that story in his own paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he was himself writing articles about the order, you say, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: He did not write an article about the order; he wrote articles about the witness that was the subject of the order. And if you look at your screen, you can see his name as the author of the article. This is the protected witness, and so what you have is one article that has the transcript of the testimony of the protected witness, which is done each day because the paper has said: Until we publish the entire transcript, we're going to continue to publish on a daily basis the transcript of this witness because we don't recognise the cease and desist order served on us by the Tribunal. And here Mr. Marijacic is writing an article about that same witness in the same pages right next to the transcript. So it's clear -- I mean, the inference you can make, I think the easy inference you can make is that he would have read and known about the order, and that's the only thing that we're trying to draw out of this. The only inference we need to make is that he's aware of this witness, this witness is the subject of this series of articles, he would have been aware of the article served on the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, were proceedings taken against these newspapers at the time for contempt of court?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Can I go into closed session -- or private session on that particular question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the indictment was brought. It is public, exclusively against Mr. Jovic, whose lead counsel I am myself. Mr. Marijacic was not mentioned, neither in the investigation or the indictment. What kind of internal investigation are we talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I think needs to be explored on that at the moment. The other question I have for you, Mr. Akerson, is this: Even assuming this order did apply to Mr. Marijacic, what does it add to the closed session order?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It's totally independent. It is not a cumulative order that -- each order stands on its own and a violation of each of these orders would constitute contempt. One is an oral order, one is a written order. They occur at very different times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why was it the Appeals Chamber thought there was no need to revoke that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Can you place the order back on the screen, please. Your Honour, what you're referring to is that the Prosecution for the ease of this trial had asked the Appeals Chamber to lift the protections on Mr. Van Kuijk so that we could refer to him by name. So they had to determine what protections were in place and what they needed to do to lift those protections. Now, when we looked at this December 1 order, they saw that this order pertains to protected witnesses. When they determined that by lifting the protections of the closed session order he thus is no longer protected, this order no longer applies and they don't have to change the terms of this order on its face in order to lift those protections. Those protections are lifted automatically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what the order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I -- if -- we are referring to, Your Honour, on page 4 of the order, the first paragraph that starts with "noting." I think that's what Your Honour is referring to. And then the next provision starting with "finding." And the finding paragraph, I think, is where the Court is annunciating this principle, that there are no protective measures granted under the order that may be varied pursuant to the Prosecution's request in its motion because it's just a standing order applying for protected witnesses. So if the status of protection is lifted off a witness, that order does not need to be varied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, you surely should have said that and made it clear to a simple-minded person like me that that was the rationale for the decision. All it says is that there were no additional protective measures granted under the order of the 1st of December, 2000, that may be varied. So for some reason, they seem to think that that order did not grant a protective measure that could be varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree with Your Honour. I think that's not the -- my interpretation of this is that they were deciding what they needed to change on the face of the order, and they decided they didn't need to change anything because once his status as a protected witness was lifted, that order can remain intact and yet the protections on that order were lifted. It's not -- it could be phrased as tightly as it could, but I think that's what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be so simple to say that finding that -- now that we have determined that the witness is no longer protected or that his testimony transcripts may be referred to publicly and in open session. There's no need to vary this, but that's not what it says, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I agree it would have been preferable if they had used that simple language. But they did not. I don't think it's clear either way, Your Honour. I think if you wanted to draw the inference of the interpretation that you're suggesting, I don't think that's clear either from the language. I think just the language of the order doesn't lend itself to an absolute interpretation either way, but I think the best conclusion that could be drawn from that provision is the one that I'm suggesting here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I have just discussed the knowledge that Mr. Marijacic had of the December 1, 2000, order and how it applies to him. I'm going to very briefly talk about Mr. Rebic's knowledge. You have in evidence three articles in front of you, November 18th, 2004, May 5th, 2005, and the HINA article of April 27th, and they all very clearly point to the fact that there was a deliberate discussion and collaboration between Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic about the application of these protection orders and whether or not to go ahead and publish. Mr. Marijacic in particular states that we had a discussion and we decided to go ahead and publish. And in the original article they said they opted to publish as well, so there's a clear indication that they had discussed and then decided to go ahead and publish, in defiance of the court order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which order? Do you say that they mentioned a third order in that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: My argument -- my submission to you, Your Honour, is that because Marijacic clearly knew of the December 1, 2000, order, that, when they had a discussion about a singular topic, which is what orders apply to this and should we go ahead and publish in defiance of those orders, of course they would have discussed the December 1, 2000, order. It's the only thing that was the topic of their discussion. And so Mr. Rebic would have been participating in a discussion about that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a serious submission, is it, that we can infer from the fact that -- that they discussed the fact that the evidence was protected and that they would be publishing in defiance of court orders, that we must read into that that the third order was specifically discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's a serious submission, and I think that's a logical inference that can be drawn from that. And if you look at the screen, Your Honour, they not only state that they've delivered it, but they say they've pondered at length the pros and cons of publishing it. They had to have included the only two -- the order that they had specific knowledge of, which is the oral order and the transcript they possessed and the written order of December 1. So I will conclude -- I have discussed now the written order and the oral order and the clear publication of the statement of Mr. Van Kuijk and his identity, how it violates both of these orders. One of the issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it -- sorry. Is it arguable that the third order applies only to the two newspapers named in it? I recollect -- now, I can't identify the number of it at the moment, but one of the exhibits includes the notification that the Tribunal sent to the Republic of Croatia to intimate the orders on the two newspapers, Globus and Slobodna, and that says that this order relates to these two particular newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is it arguable that the order only applied to these two newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's a reasonable inference. I think the principle of law is that if someone has knowledge of an order that has a broad provision like this, which expresses a Court's clear intent to protect information, when they have knowledge of that order and their intent is to violate that order by publishing the protected information, that that order then applies to them. It has to apply to them, we would submit. And my final point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you resume, can I clarify this issue. It seems to me that you are arguing on the basis of the closed session order and the 1st of December, 2000, order.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if this means that you are not any longer seeking to argue on the basis of the first order, that is the first -- the 6th of June, 1997 order. So can I take it to be a kind of concession?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The issue was raised yesterday about: Is this a serious interference, and I think that's the last point that I want to address here today. As I've said, closed session is the most severe -- the most serious form of protection this Tribunal can give to a witness. It's where a witness's identity -- everything about that witness is protected. We draw a curtain down so the audience can't see anything about that witness. The public is totally excluded, so its very nature is, in most circumstances, to protect everything about that witness, including his identity. And I want to read a quote from the Aleksovski contempt decision, page 8. This is the Appeals Chamber, which says: "A decision of the Trial Chamber relating to the protection of witnesses, which may be written or oral," that's their language, "may be written or oral is of the utmost importance, not only for the lives of the witnesses, but also for the operations of the Tribunal. "On November 18th, the accused knowingly published the identity and statement of a witness who had received the Tribunal's strongest protections." They openly challenged those protections, and the OTP considers this to be a serious interference with our ability to convince witnesses who are being asked to testify in Croatian cases, in particular, that when they come and we promise them that they will have confidentiality, that that means something, that this Court stands behind it, and we protect those witnesses with every ounce of our ability to do so, and this clearly shows an interference with the Tribunal's administration of justice, and we would therefore ask you to find Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic guilty of contempt of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. Shall we adjourn sometime before we hear from the Defence closing arguments? Do you have anything to clarify? I wonder whether your colleague has brought something to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And I haven't seen it yet, so I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, thanks to the help of the Registry, was able to obtain final list of witnesses in the Blaskic case, which includes pseudonym for Mr. Van Kuijk, and I will distribute these. There's a confidential and a public version, and his identity is protected in both of these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who made the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: This is the final registry list of witnesses in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Made by the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Correct. And his -- the pseudonym that was assigned to Mr. Van Kuijk was EE and we've searched the trial transcripts. There's only one reference to Witness EE in the trial, and that's in the Defence closing argument which takes place on July 30th, 1999, and we've searched the judgement of the Blaskic case, and there's no reference to either van Kuijk or EE, just to confirm what's been previously stated. And I want to remind the Court that there's already in evidence which is Exhibit P13, which is the Prosecution's ex parte, in camera motion, request for a hearing in respect of the evidence of newly discovered evidence, and that it was a motion by the Prosecution to support its request that Mr. Van Kuijk be added as a witness; he was not previously known to the Defence. That's P13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the OTP number?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: 4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Tab 13 would be 2, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would there be anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Tab 13, volume 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would there be anything to indicate that the designation of Mr. Van Kuijk as Witness EE was anything more than administrative action taken by the Registry? Is there anything to suggest that this was confirmed by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or ordered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The fact, Your Honour, that the Defence referred to the witness by the name -- the pseudonym is evidence that it was being used in the trial. It was used in the closing argument. They refer to him not by name but by his pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you draw my attention, please, to where on the list of witnesses there is reference to Morillon and Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If you will -- if you can give me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you have in front of you is just the Prosecution witness list. The two witnesses you referred to are Chamber witnesses, and so we'll have to get that list. I have here, Your Honour, the Chamber witness list, but we don't have copies. So we'll have to ask the Registry to make copies for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it specifically name both of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, do you know whether this list was made up before the closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't say with a certainty that the list was made before the closing arguments but the pseudonym clearly existed before the closing argument because it could not have been used unless it was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And do you have anything to clarify how that pseudonym came into existence, whether -- with judicial authority or whether it was just an administrative action by the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think the official court record ultimately was the list of witnesses, as you have it in front of you. I don't have any document which shows how these pseudonyms were assigned. I don't have that in my possession to provide to the Court. But it would be very surprising to me that it was an informal arrangement between the parties and the Defence counsel, just by agreement with Prosecution, had decided to assign a pseudonym and used it, because the Court wouldn't have had an idea of who that witness was. There had to have been an official agreement, we just don't have that document in front of us. But we do have -- I mean, it's -- there's almost incontrovertible evidence that if they're using it in the closing argument and everyone understands who that witness is, everyone had to have had the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is clear is that during testimony he was not called EE. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Correct. When Mr. Van Kuijk testified, when they argued in favour of him being allowed to testify in closed session, they just referred to him as "the witness." In closed session they referred to him with his name, but they never used EE at that time. I have copies of the page where he's referenced, and it also further clarifies that it's a Dutch -- it says here: "This was the testimony of Witness EE. It's a Dutch name that I cannot pronounce well," and this is at transcript page 5531, so they're referring back to this witness. So it's very clear that's who it is. If I could have this contributed, please. It's very clear that this is van Kuijk, he is van Kuijk, which corroborates the list that you have in front of you, the registry list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that submission made in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, I have also tried to gather some information, but it's absolutely clear to me now. As you can see, on the secret list from the Prosecution, it is written clearly for the first time in the upper right-hand corner when that was distributed, and that was just before closing arguments. On the 18th September, 1998, it says, and it's absolutely clear to me that before that time there was no use of pseudonym, because it was only received on that date. It is confirmed also by the transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I have here, what the Prosecutor gave to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We don't have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: You don't have this document; I'm happy to provide it to you. I went to the senior trial attorney to ask about this list. He provided his own personal copy, and he's got a note in the upper right-hand corner with the date of September 18th, 1998. Now, the closing argument was July 30th, 1999. So it's ten months -- this document in our internal file is handwritten with a date that's ten months before the closing argument. So it would suggest -- I was not going to provide this because it's handwritten. I don't know who wrote this date; it's just from our internal file. But as long as Defence counsel is introducing it, this tends to suggest that this existed at least ten months before the closing argument. But I will add, I have never asserted here that at the time that Mr. Van Kuijk testified that he testified with a pseudonym. That's never been our argument. We've never asserted any written or oral pleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I regret the Prosecution was not able to produce this document during the Prosecution's case, but I'll hear from Mr. Krsnik. Do you have anything further in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at this transcript that was just provided by our learned friend, I've read it - of course my English is not perfect - but it follows very clearly that Defence counsel has trouble with pronunciation, and that's the only reason he's using "EE." That's the first and the last time that EE was used. There is no evidence that this -- these initials were used before or after, at least that's how I understood the English text. And of course, in my closing arguments I will provide you with this copy. I think it would be fair and just for you to see for yourselves what is written in the right-hand upper corner. Another point, Your Honour. I was working at the Tribunal even then. The closing argument took six months to prepare. That was the time allowed, and I am sure that this was purely an administrative measure by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, how do you like the Chamber to treat these documents? What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We would ask that these be moved into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, at this time. They're self-authenticating court records and we think that they assist the court in making a determination in this case. In response to what the Defence just submitted, that Witness EE was just used spontaneously, the record is very clear that if -- in closing argument in an important trial, if this was not agreed upon as a pseudonym that all parties recognised, the Court and/or the Prosecution would have objected to the use of the name. Everyone knew what was going on; it's very clear from the record. I think it's an implausible suggestion to suggest that this was a spontaneous utterance of the witness's name. So I will -- that's my submission on that. I think it's very clear from the record that this Registry list reflected what was known by the parties at the time they made the closing arguments, and you have the date, the informal date, on the Prosecution's file. You can give that whatever weight you want. I was not intending to tender that, but I think the Court should see it because the Defence has raised it and I'll as that this be admitted into evidence as well. But all the evidence you have in front of you suggests very clearly that this is an official pseudonym that was recognised by everybody, including the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the only thing that can be relevant is the decision of the Trial Chamber. Why didn't the OTP provide it? Because they don't have it. In that case, I submit that we should adjourn in order to obtain their decision. That is the only thing that can be relevant, but we are now at the stage of closing arguments. I don't think that new evidence can be even presented for admission at this stage. But if there is any evidence that is relevant is that decision of the Trial Chamber. I don't think it's a problem to find it. If they found this one, why couldn't they find it? They are well resourced. Of course they have even the software necessary. It must be in the computer. What is clear is that that decision does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from Mr. Akerson, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents were obtained from the Registry at the request of Your Honours, who had asked us to retrieve these documents. So we provided this at your request, and if you would feel more comfortable then it seems more appropriate that it is given a Trial Court Exhibit Number, because these documents were requested by you and provided to you at your request. Secondly, the Defence, their objection that we can't add new evidence at this stage. Yesterday, despite the fact that this case has been litigated without any new issues, it's been pending for six months. It's a very simple case. They, yesterday, said that they may list - I can't remember the exact phrase - but it was a lot of witnesses. They can't at the one hand say, Well, we may need to list a lot of new witnesses and on the other hand say, Well, we can't respond to the Court's request to retrieve official court documents that you've requested. These are documents that are relevant to this case, you've requested that we provide them to you. They are completely self-authenticating and the most important principle here is that they help you decide on facts, the guilt or innocence of the parties in this case. And by -- on that standard, especially on the standard of relevance, they should be admitted, given whatever weight you deem necessary, and then used in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you concede that there was no court order preceding these -- at least the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I will concede that I'm not aware of a court order. We've searched, but there's material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you can't find any order?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, we haven't been able to find any order preceding this. Obviously we would have provided it because we ran searches and we would have provided it if we found it. That being been said, the record-keeping is not always stellar at the Tribunal, and it's not to say it doesn't exist, but we've made searches, good-faith searches to find it and have not been able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just one additional point that I think is relevant, which is that we -- in a contempt case, we are actually prosecuting this on your behalf. This is not our own Prosecution. We were given an order directing the Prosecutor to investigate contempt, but this is really your prosecution of contempt because you're enforcing your own inherent power. So there is no limitation of what you receive into evidence, because this is not a classic adversarial proceeding, this is your enforcement of your own inherent power and you should not limit yourself, I would submit, to what evidence is useful in making a determination of whether or not Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic committed contempt. That is the only thing that matters, is the evidence relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have still anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I have something to say. I simply can't help saying it. I've tried to learn something about rhetorics and the common law systems, although I'm trying not to get on my feet and object to every comment. But what the Prosecutor just said is not correct, simply not correct. It was an initiative from the OTP; they did not have an order from the Trial Chamber, especially not the Trial Chamber presided by Judge Jorda. They wanted an investigation and they submitted an indictment to the Judge on duty. And they invoked Article -- Rule 75. The Trial Chamber did not initiate this investigation. Moreover, the Trial Chamber didn't want that investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, the Chamber is all aware -- aware of all the situation. The Chamber will make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber, by a majority, will admit these documents into evidence pursuant to 98, Rule 98, as a Chamber exhibit. That does not necessarily mean that the Chamber admits there was a protected -- there was an order granting that kind of pseudonym. The Chamber will leave it as an open question whether there was an order from the Trial Chamber or whether the identity of the witness was protected as -- via pseudonym. So those exhibits will be given a Chamber exhibit number. There are several of them. Why don't we admit them all as well as the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, for the clarification. So the bundle of exhibits is comprised of the list of the Registry officially provided to OTP today, confidential and public. This also is comprised of the list of pseudonym of witnesses, as provided by OTP to Your Honour. And finally, the transcript. Thank you, Your Honour. And this will be given the exhibit number C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't we deal with the transcript separately and giving it a separate number for C2. And Judge Bonomy will pronounce his position briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wish to explain briefly why I would not permit these documents to be exhibited at this stage. I'm extremely grateful to Mr. Akerson for giving us the full picture and indicating what is available in relation to a pseudonym, but the only way in which the pseudonym could be of any relevance in this case, in my opinion, would be if it was applied as a result of a court order. This case is about the breach of court orders; there's no evidence of such an order, and therefore all these documents, in my opinion, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having done that, we'll hear from the Defence their closing arguments, starting from Mr. Ivanovic for Mr. Ivica Marijacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to address you. Here when we are talking about the indictment against Ivica Marijacic, we have to bear in mind that Ivica Marijacic is a professional journalist. His job includes the right to inform the public. It is his duty, in fact, that while performing his job he should inform the public about hearings before this Tribunal. The right to a public trial is a right guaranteed by Article 21 of the Statute of this Tribunal itself, and it stipulates clearly that everything that is not explicitly designated as secret or confidential should be accessible to the public so that the public should have an insight into the workings of this Tribunal. Ivica Marijacic could never have known or checked whether the witness statement is secret. Let me remind you of what a Prosecution witness we had has said. On the witness statement itself, there is no mark of confidentiality. Therefore, this Trial Chamber, following the request of the OTP, should be the first Trial Chamber of this Tribunal that would find criminally liable a journalist who was only doing his job. Do the facts that we have heard in the past two days support this? In our submission, Your Honour, no. What was Ivica Marijacic charged with? Strictly with violation of a court order of this Tribunal. Under the order of the Tribunal of the 16th of January, 2006, not the 6th of July -- June, sorry, 1997, it is very clear that there is no violation, even of the order of the 1st December, 2000. The order of the 1st December invokes the order of the 6th of June, 1997. Why cannot the order of the 1st December apply to Ivica Marijacic? It cannot because the Appeals Chamber itself in its findings of the 16th of January says that there is nothing to vary in that order because nothing new was added. The decision of the 6th of June clearly defines that protective measures are granted to witnesses residing in the former Yugoslavia. The Appeals Chamber found that Witness van Kuijk did not reside in the former Yugoslavia. For all those reasons, it is clear that neither the order of the 1st December nor the others can apply to Mr. Marijacic because that order gives no particular protection to Witness van Kuijk. There remains outstanding the question of the order to proceed in closed session on the 19th of December. The first thing I would like to stress is the following: Ivica Marijacic or the Hrvatski List newspaper did not publish a single word from the closed session. This was also confirmed by a Prosecution witness here. Furthermore, the Prosecution claims that the principle is at stake, namely, not to allow anyone to second-guess decisions of the Tribunal. As a human being, I absolutely agree with this, but those decisions must be clear and clearly defined, not only for lawyers but also for the public. This decision to proceed in closed session unfortunately does not meet that standard. Not a single part of that decision reflects the previous decision dating back four months earlier. It does not explicitly proclaim the contents secret or protected, neither for the parties or the Trial Chamber. Whose duty is it to see to it? The party that seeks protective measures, in this case the Prosecution. It could also be the duty of the Trial Chamber, maybe someone else as well; but it is certainly not the duty of a professional journalist to see to it that court decisions are clearly defined and understandable to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, surely one issue that is clear in this case is that whether or not the identity of a witness is protected by a closed session order, his evidence is protected by the order. Can there really be any argument to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour, and I am continuing to say so in my closing remarks. His testimony in closed session is protected. But Ivica Marijacic and Hrvatski List did not publish a single word from the closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just take it stage by stage. Mr. Marijacic, in writing his article, clearly knew that he was breaching the order. It's clear from the article that that's what he was deliberately setting out to do, and your submission must be consistent, obviously, with that position or you must indicate to us, I would suggest, some basis for thinking that he made some mistake. Is that what you're suggesting, that he had made a mistake about the effect of the order or what? I don't understand it. The evidence is clear about what he thought he was doing, and it's rather technical to suggest: Well, he didn't provide the transcript word-for-word because he provided, by using the statement, the same information and then he's called it the transcript. It all looks very devious on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. With your leave I will explain. Ivica Marijacic published parts of the statement that bears no mark of confidentiality. Ivica Marijacic is not somebody who sat before this Trial Chamber. He couldn't have been familiar with the order of the Trial Chamber made in closed session. Ivica Marijacic received and published what was published as a fax transmission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What order was he talking about then that made his -- this secret evidence? What on earth was he talking about in the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood that article, Your Honour, Ivica Marijacic did not mention a single specific order of this Tribunal. Ivica Marijacic probably, checking things on the Internet, saw that there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
