utterances.text: It's not for you to speculate. I want you to concentrate on the evidence. On the basis of the evidence, what on earth can this Trial Chamber conclude other than that this publication was meant to defy a court order here that made this secret testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to repeat. Ivica Marijacic and Hrvatski List did not publish a single word from a material clearly designated as protected or secret. What is marked as protected, namely closed session material, is the transcript of the testimony. Of that, Ivica Marijacic did not publish a single word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hear what you say. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that there are no marks of confidentiality on the statement itself, and we heard that from a person who knows about these things, from a witness from the Prosecution. That conclusion, therefore, that this would allow anyone to second-guess court orders is unjustified, especially with regard to journalists. Let me remind you again, my client never received a single direct order. All other parties have been cautioned, but not my client. And now the Prosecution asks you, Your Honours, to find my client guilty of contempt. Is that fair? This case is very clear. The Office of the Prosecutor did not provide any evidence to support the claim that my client violated any direct order of this Tribunal for the simple reason that there was no such direct order issued to him. Why shouldn't he be subjected to measures that are applied to all the other journalists? Your Honour, this begs the question: How did the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case react in other cases? I believe the spirit of the decision of the Court is clearly expressed in their decisions regarding witnesses Thebault and Morillon. In their cases, the Trial Chamber very clearly decided that those witnesses would be testifying in closed session, that all prior statements of those witnesses should be regarded as confidential. But is their identity secret? No. Where is such a decision in the case of Witness van Kuijk? There is no such decision. The Prosecution invokes the decision to proceed in closed session. I repeat, Ivica Marijacic did not violate their decision, but nothing, no part of that closed session, was published in Hrvatski List. This further brings us to another question: How could Ivica Marijacic, a professional journalist, know that nine years later the Prosecution will assume the stance that such a statement, a witness statement, that is in no way marked as secret, given by a witness who never asked for any protective measures, as admitted by the Prosecution itself, would become secret only by virtue of a later decision that this witness should testify in closed session? How could Ivica Marijacic have known that the Prosecution will take this position? There was no way he could have known. Why did the Trial Chamber proceed in closed session in the first place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He wrote, Mr. Ivanovic, that Mr. Rebic gave him the two documents. He asked him: "Are these protected documents?" And the answer was: "These are protected documents and I am aware of the possible consequences of making them public." So whatever might be said about whether that's evidence against Mr. Rebic, it's undoubtedly evidence against Mr. Marijacic. I'm fully aware that they were protected documents. Now, he's chosen not to answer that by not giving evidence, and therefore what other conclusion can one draw but that he knew they were protected documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to this question of yours, I would just like to say the following: Mr. Marijacic knows that Mr. Rebic also had not been involved in proceedings before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Blaskic Trial Chamber is very clear on that. The decision was passed because of the sensitivity of the evidence in respect of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. So the state expressed its interest, its concern, that some statement could affect the national interests of that country. The said state intervenes and seeks protective measures. The high officer was not present on the 1st and 2nd of August, 1997, when testimony was given, but he was present at the closed session in December the same year. In my opinion, this clearly shows the attitude of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, that the statement itself did not jeopardise the interest of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It was also possible that perhaps in broader evidence in session, the interests of the Kingdom of the Netherlands could be affected, but never mind. There's only one thing that's certain, and it was also heard from the Prosecution witnesses and from the Prosecutor himself. Not a single one of the reasons for which the session was closed existed when the text was published in Hrvatski List. There is just one more additional question. As for van Kuijk's testimony, why did the Trial Chamber not reach a clear-cut decision, as in the case of General Morillon and Mr. Thebault? Why were things left this ambiguous? We don't know that and we also don't know who is responsible for that; the only thing we do know for sure is that Ivica Marijacic is not responsible for that. I call upon this Trial Chamber not to allow, due to the omissions of others, to have my client proclaimed guilty. He did his job, and he believed that modern democracy rests on the public nature of many things, like this Tribunal. And that can be explained by the following principle: That everything that is not marked as secret and confidential is public. That is a lofty right and it is one of the fundamental human rights. The Statute of this court guarantees it as a foremost pattern of behaviour. In my opinion, the Office of the Prosecutor cannot be allowed to decide arbitrarily on something seven years after things have happened; that has to be stated quite clearly at the moment when things are actually done, when they happen, just like it was clearly marked in the case of General Morillon and Mr. Thebault. Finally, Your Honour, I would like to remind you once again of the key fact, perhaps, in these proceedings. Ivica Marijacic is the only accused journalist before this Tribunal who never got an order to cease doing what he was doing, especially not in the van Kuijk list and in the case of Hrvatski List. All other journalists and newspapers got a direct warning, and in spite of it continued to violate the rules of the Tribunal. And I'm sure that the OTP will be able to prove that very quickly before this Trial Chamber. So, Your Honours, Ivica Marijacic did not violate the order of the 6th of June, 1997. He did not violate the order of the 1st of December, 2000. He did not violate the order of the closed session because he did not publish anything from there. He jeopardised no one by his text, let alone van Kuijk or the interests of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and Ivica Marijacic was the only journalist who was indicted here without being given previous warning, as all other accused journalists were. I am profoundly convinced that this Trial Chamber will protect the human and professional rights as a journalist of Ivica Marijacic and will not sacrifice them to the ambitions of the Office of the Prosecutor, that arbitrarily decides on what is secret and what is not secret. Furthermore, I wish to believe that this Trial Chamber will take into account the fact that in this case the evidence produced was not sufficient for this Trial Chamber to reach a first precedent in the work of the International Criminal Tribunal by proclaiming guilty a professional who simply did his job. The OTP wishes to limit the rights of a journalist, and in this way to impose restrictions on the rights of the public. Please, Your Honours, on the basis of these facts, do not turn Ivica Marijacic from a professional journalist into a criminal; that would absolutely not be proper and fair. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try to be as brief as possible, and I'll try to be as reasonable as possible. Actually, I don't want to go into any big-time debate here. It doesn't involve some kind of great wisdom. What this is all about is an ordinary, everyday legal issue. The legal issue is whether my client committed the crime of contempt of court and whether our learned friends of the Prosecution submitted sufficient evidence of this because they bear the burden of proof, and have they proven all this beyond a reasonable doubt? As far as I can see and as far as I managed to feel on the basis of these proceedings over the past two days, many arbitrary conclusions were drawn and many arbitrary opinions were reached, apart from legal arguments, if you wish. I have something to say that has to do with legal arguments, and indeed I'm going to say that. The real reason for this indictment is a show of force on the part of the Prosecution, especially the Prosecutor himself repeated twice that this was due to the preparation of two big cases. Imagine, that's supposed to be an argument for us, an argument in terms of whether there was a violation of a Rule. However, since the Prosecutor brought this up, I would like to tell you that that is, in fact, what the Prosecution thinks. And you know why? It's very simple. And now I'm going to give you an example of that. Please let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As I understood the point the Prosecutor was making was that if the protection of the protective measures that are granted by the Tribunal are seen to be ineffective, then that will actively discourage or at least raise the risk of discouraging potential witnesses from committing themselves to come to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was my understanding, too. But I also understood in my own way the interpretation of the gentleman of the Prosecution, that they do wish to show force. Because if this were so, then they would have dealt with all violations from the press from the former Yugoslavia in the same way, and there were at least 100 such cases. However, not a single indictment was issued. Now that you're asking me, Your Honour. Judge Bonomy, I've been listening very carefully to your wise comments, sensical remarks, and please don't think that I'm trying to flatter you in any way. But why would Hrvatski List be indicted and not Globos Vjesnik [phoen] who violated or the editors of the newspapers were aware of the fact that they were violating the Rules and they said they would go on doing that. It's only Novi List that was indicted, Hrvatski List and Slobodna Dalmacija; no one else. Hundreds of newspapers. What about Defence witnesses who are protected? In cases where I was Defence counsel, practically all of my protected witnesses had their names disclosed. And I wanted to have a debate on this and I was not allowed to have one. We did not have any hearings on that. The Prosecutor said no. And now the OTP is terribly worried. About what, Your Honours? What are they worried about? They never sought protective measures for this witness, but it was the Dutch government that did. There is a valid judgement. In this case for years there has been no Dutch Battalion in Bosnia, and the Dutch government is not asking for anything now, but it was the Prosecutor who had to apply the same standards and the same procedure like all the rest of us. They have to observe the same rules. So what does that mean, Your Honours? That no one on earth may ever publish anything, if we are to apply what the Prosecutor said just now. And what are students going to study in the future about this Tribunal? And what will history write about? If something is not common sensical, then it cannot be right, fair, and just. The law cannot move against common sense. The question here is: Was this witness in jeopardy or not? We all know that the witness was not jeopardised. Your Honours, the OTP wants a precedent. They want to have your ruling that they can wave in front of all. They certainly have their own hidden intentions. Of course I'm engaging in guesswork now, I'm sorry, I am convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you are departing from your own norm of presenting a simple, common sensical legal argument, or everyday legal argument, as you said. That's only half of the issue, Mr. Krsnik, the other half of the issue is whether the material itself was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am defending Mr. Rebic, and he's been indicted for two things, and you simplified matters by making a single point on this: Disclosure of identity of a protected witness and the transcript. I have a very simple answer to that. I could have called Mr. Rebic to the stand, if this is what I thought. He could have come to testify here in front of you and say: No, I did not give the transcript. I am putting a concrete question to you. Are you really going to take newspapers as evidence from a part of the world that is still learning journalism and law and democracy? Hrvatski List is not the Washington Post, you know, but the Washington Post was the first one to carry the story about Cicko Bralo. You have to know the background about all of this. The distinguished lady, Ms. Carla del Ponte, threatened to turn to the Security Council of the UN and accuse Croatia of hiding Cicko Bralo and Mr. Rebic of doing that. And now when you see van Kuijk's statement, you see that that was not true. There was a tempest. The Croatian media reported on this for days, and Hrvatski List was one of the newspapers that wrote an article on this. So that's the background. But let me simplify matters even further. I think that the Office of the Prosecutor did not prove in these proceedings, not with a shred of evidence -- this is my position, Your Honours. Attorneys are usually prone to exaggeration and they like to impress their clients; that's not the kind of person I am. And I am stating very clearly that the Prosecution did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that my client disclosed any identity or the transcript, well, except for the newspapers. If that is sufficient evidence for you, then I know what awaits me. But if newspapers, newspaper articles, are not sufficient, I know what's in store, again. But I know something else. I am asking for a precedent from this Trial Chamber because this is a very sensitive matter. What is at stake is the right of the public to information. Your Honours, maybe you don't know this. You are sitting here, vested with this great authority from the international community. But the eyes of the public in the former Yugoslavia are directed at you, awaiting your every word and decision. One of the proclaimed principles is that this Tribunal should contribute to the restoration of peace in that region. You can set a precedent and say that if an order does not have clear enough wording, that there is no clear protection, then there was no violation of those orders. And it is my position that Mr. Rebic did not violate any of the said orders. And third, we need a clearly expressed position from you as to when there is and when there isn't contempt of court. I have one more point to make, and that is the application of Rule 77. The Prosecutor keeps invoking it the way he understands it and I, of course, understand that he has his own approach; that's his right. Rule 77 could not be any clearer, particularly in point (C). Of course I'm not going to point it because you know it. But Rule 77(A)(ii) clearly says that: "Any person who discloses information relating to those proceedings in knowing violation of an order of a Chamber," it is up to say whether there was violation, whether it was violated by Mr. Rebic, and, if there was violation, then of which order. It is my position that the fact alone that the session was closed does not mean protection. That is a very exclusive interpretation adopted by the Prosecution, but we will hear your answers. If protection existed, then it would have been granted by an order of the Trial Chamber. And if we had -- if we had that order, the Prosecution would certainly be parading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What then do you say, Mr. Krsnik, is the alternative interpretation of going into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have spent a lot of time in these courtrooms, as have you, and you know exactly how it happens that closed sessions are used. What was at stake in our case was protection of military secrets of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; there was no other reasons, there was no other reason. If there had been, they would have been clearly stated in a court order. And that is why the Kingdom of the Netherlands, once the DutchBat came back, had to ask for these measures to be lifted without leaving it in the hands of the Prosecutor. Although it is, properly speaking, the job of the Prosecutor. The Prosecution cannot hold the key as to who is in contempt and who isn't, because if you decide that everything they say is secret, then you give them the power --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't understand the point. It was left to the Dutch government to ask for the measures to be lifted. And did they ask for the measures to be lifted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. Cameron confirmed that. The Dutch government asked for the protection to be lifted, and this was confirmed by Mr. Cameron. It is also in the statement of Mr. Cameron that I provided. I will give you the page, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that this may be a translation problem. The Dutch government asked for the measures to be imposed. It's been translated as "asked for them to be lifted."

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I can clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Just a minute. I will explain. The question is directed at me, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my closing argument he had made several objections. He's misstating fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, let's -- I can clear it up with him, and if it remains unclear then, when he's finished, you can say what you wish to say in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is: During the trial in 1997, the Dutch government asked for protective measures because of the sensitivity of their military operations. In 2005, the Dutch government asked the Office of the Prosecutor to list those measures because the reason for their imposition no longer exists. And that is stated in the witness statement and in the testimony of Witness Cameron. I questioned him about it, and he confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have his statement, so we should be able to check that. I have no recollection of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the penultimate page in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have that statement. If Mr. Akerson can help us in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: You don't have the statement in evidence, but what you do have is the motion for the lifting of protective measures, which does clarify. Because the Dutch government did not ask the OTP to lift the protective measures. We asked them, in light of this Trial Chamber, if they would consent to lifting the protective measures, which was put in the motion for lifting of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's my recollection, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I will find it. Just give me a little time. I'll find the statement where it is clearly written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In case of a -- Mr. Cameron's statement, only the cover page was put on the ELMO and was not handed over to the Chamber. So we received Tomljanovich's statement, but not Cameron's, Mr. Cameron's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, Your Honour. I have the Croatian version only; I don't have the English version. In the Croatia version, it's page 4, paragraph 5. It reads -- I will read slowly, and I will appreciate the help of the interpreters. I gave you the statement yesterday but not today. I am reading from the statement prepared by Mr. Cameron himself, and for the record we call it "statement given to the OTP." It reads: "On the 27th October, 2005, I received an electronic communication from the Dutch Ministry of Defence which authorised the International Criminal Tribunal to have the record of Mr. Van Kuijk's testimony placed in the public domain and to remove protective measures in regard of Captain van Kuijk. Source: Terrence Cameron."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that not in response to the Prosecution's request whether they agree or object to the lifting of the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see that here. I see that this is an initiative from the Ministry of Defence. It is not written anywhere that this could be a reply to the request of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution's motion to the Appeals Chamber requesting a variation of protective measures, i.e., the lifting of the protective measures in relation to Witness van Kuijk was filed on 2nd of November in 2005. And I noticed from your reading of this, Mr. Cameron's statement, he received the communication from Dutch Ministry of Defence on 27th of October. So one can assume that that communication was in response to the question of the Prosecution. Am I correct? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Prosecution filed this motion after receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, after the receiving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the Dutch government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to you it is an open question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- whether the Prosecution asked the Dutch government whether they agree or not with the lifting of the protective measures? Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am glad we have clarified this. So it was the initiative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, not the OTP. And that is the reason why I am asking this Court not to allow the Prosecution to do this, but, on the contrary, to send them a message, to protect the right to a fair and public trial. And that whenever we have measures that are more than -- that go outside the scope of the reasonable, that they should be the ones to ask for the lifting of such measures. Because the OTP should not be allowed to have sole discretion in these matters. What actually happened in this Tribunal? You know the original order in 1996. The Court dismissed their motion to investigate and never allowed an investigation. The Duty Judge considered this motion and rejected it. I studied this, and I know from Rule 77 that it is the exclusive right of the Trial Chamber to decide on contempt of court. And I would be grateful if you would support it in your decision. I'm not going to elaborate on the right of the media and the right to information, especially information from this Tribunal, but doesn't it seem to you that if we read carefully Rule 75(A), which does not even limit the rights of the accused, it always takes care to protect the rights of the accused. If we started interpreting it as the Prosecutor does, wouldn't that jeopardise the rights of all parties, or at least considerably limit those rights, including the rights of the media and the freedom of the media. I'm stressing for the 15th time, from every common sensical point of view, the behaviour of my client did not put anyone in danger. I do not wish to take anymore of your time. I don't wish to refer to the testimony of Mr. Tomljanovich. I will just say that my client, Mr. Rebic, until his retirement on the 26th of February, when he handed over his duty, that was the 26th of February, 2000, and he has been retired to date, but since unfortunately in Croatia retirement pensions are not very high and he is, by primary occupation, professor of philosophy with a Ph.D. in philosophy, he freelances as a journalist in Hrvatski List as a writer, as a contributor. While he was assistant minister of defence for security, he displayed a high level of awareness, and I thank my colleagues from the OTP for giving us a chance to hear Mr. Tomljanovich, that gave us a chance to compare various performances. He closely protected every document he handled, always making sure to mark them as confidential if they were confidential. The fact that the Prosecution got hold of these documents - and I'm impressed with the job they did in obtaining them from the Croatian state - in Croatia he would be punished much more severely than here for allowing the disclosure of such documents. And now imagine, for 15 years, from 1991 to 2004, Mr. Markica Rebic did not disclose anything to anyone because he was liable, both before the national legislation and the international community, the international legislation. And the Prosecution has suggested that he suddenly did in 2001. But even if that was so - and if I am proven wrong, I will always suffer from pangs of conscience for not doing my job well and not putting him on the stand - I will never forgive myself if you find him guilty of contempt based on the evidence that I believe is clearly insufficient with regard to my client. Through these days I have always been guided by one thought: We have to be serious in our job. I always tried not to put my clients on the stand or even to produce character witnesses. I think we have learned the truth just by hearing the Prosecution case, which is insufficient. And now my eyes are upon you. I had the privilege and honour of acting as Defence counsel before such a Trial Chamber as this that can often be seen on Croatian television. And I thank you for your patience, and I hope that my client will be acquitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. I have to ask Mr. Akerson whether you have anything for rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, a few short comments. Do you want to take a break first or would you like me to proceed right into that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I -- five or ten minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I just need a moment to get my podium set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While my colleague is getting ready, may I just say something? There's something I think the Trial Chamber has to know. It is the clients who are paying themselves for these big expenses of appearing before this Court, the hotels, the plane tickets. They are truly financially exhausted. They even had to get credits in order to pay for all these costs because the registry turned them down. I'm asking this Trial Chamber kindly: Could your ruling be -- well, I don't know, perhaps I'm asking for something that is truly out of the ordinary, but could you please rule today if at all possible? Or, when you do rule, could we please hear the decision by videolink so that this does not incur major expenses again? Of course you don't have to answer me now, but I simply felt it necessary to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I don't think it is for the Chamber to rule on any financial matters. It is for the Registry, and I have to consult with my colleagues whether the accused can appear on videolink. But I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, I just want to respond to a very small point, but it's a misstatement of fact regarding the Dutch government and who requested that protection measures be lifted. I will turn your attention to what is the decision on the Prosecution's motion for the variance of protection measures in this case, page 4, last paragraph. It says in this motion that: "According to the Prosecution, neither the witness van Kuijk nor the Dutch Ministry of Defence have any objection to the relief requested in this motion." Now, the timing of this is important because this -- the allegation is here the Dutch government contacted us and asked to have the protections lifted. This is right before trial. And either the Dutch government spontaneously of their own initiative somehow came to this conclusion, or, as it's clear I think from this motion, that we asked them to lift this so that we could conduct a trial in a reasonable way without having to worry about witness protections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if was it October 2004, it might have been relevant, but I have to say I fail to see the relevance of any -- who did what in October 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I totally agree. I totally agree it's irrelevant, but I'll get to the main point that Mr. Marijacic said this is a case of freedom of the press. It's not a case about freedom of the press. Clearly that is a paramount principle; however, we also recognise that there are limitations on freedoms in the press. There's the law of defamation, the law of slander, the law of libel. But more importantly for us closed session testimony is a limitation on the freedom of the press. We're excluding, now, anybody who's not in this courtroom. There's a reason for that. There's a balance to be weighed. The press has a right to cover trials, and the trials should be public where possible, but Your Honours should be aware of a need to protect certain witnesses from exposure to the press. Now, neither Mr. Marijacic or Mr. Rebic was able to address the questions addressed to them about was content of closed session testimony protected. Neither one could answer that. They also couldn't answer the question -- their own admission is that they knew it was protected information. Were they somehow disavowing those statements as inaccurate? They never addressed that. What stand before you is that they both admitted that the material was protected. They haven't, in argument or in evidence, put anything before the Court's that suggests anything other than the obvious. They have admitted that these are protected -- they knew this was protected, and they published it in knowing violation that it was protected. The question is, for you, and I think it's an obvious one and the implications are great: Does closed session protect the content. Mr. Rebic through his counsel now just said: It does not. Page 58, line 16, at 11.22.55 in the transcript, page 58, line 16, 11.22.55. Judge Bonomy asked him, "Was this session -- was closed -- does that mean protection?" He said, "It does not mean protection." Now the implications of that I don't have to go into, but they are profound for us, and that's what this case is about. The Prosecution is interested in protecting the witness protective measures that exist. It's not a case about interfering with Mr. Van Kuijk. That's never an allegation that was made in any pleading, in any argument. It's an interference with our ability to guarantee witnesses who come to us only on the agreement that they will be confidential, that that means something and it's going to be enforced. And when papers knowingly violate that, that we step in and charge them with contempt and enforce it. Now, Mr. Marijacic was -- he mentioned that the closed session wasn't published. Another principle facing this Court, and I also think it's indisputable, that the evidence of a witness is protected, not the form of the evidence. A literal transcript. And he says: "Nowhere on this transcript does it say 'secret.' It does not explicitly proclaim the contents secret." And if you follow that logic, that means every transcript, every closed session -- every transcript containing closed session testimony is public by their argument because it doesn't say "secret." If closed session doesn't mean closed, closed from the public, it's public. Their argument is it's public. And I think the Court has to take the position that closed session testimony protects the evidence of a witness in whatever form. There's no other reasonable inference. Mr. Marijacic also says there was no direct order issued to his client. They admit they have possession of the transcript of the closed session order, and that order has to protect the material. And they knowingly violated that protection, and that's the essence of contempt. I have no other issues to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rule 86 - just a second, Mr. Krsnik - (C) says: "The parties shall also address matters of sentencing in closing arguments." So you have nothing further in relation to sentencing issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Only what's already on the record, Your Honour, that we consider this to be a serious violation based on the flagrant and sensational nature of how it was put in the paper and interfere with our ability and due administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence in response to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor never had a case from the very outset, and he showed that. Why? The first order - and that's when all the orders started -- I don't want to be a burden to you and I don't want to bore you, Your Honours. It only had to do with persons who resided in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. We can now interpret this any way we want. It does not pertain to van Kuijk. He never had protection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to deal with one of the matters that our learned friend from the Prosecution raised. We never said that the transcript was not marked as confidential; I'm talking about the statement of Witness van Kuijk. That was not marked as confidential in any way. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank both counsel for their helpful submission today, and the Chamber will make a decision in due course and inform the parties in due course. The hearing is now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.55 a.m.
